metadata.title: Getting Skills Right How Workers Use, or Don’t Use, their Skills in the Workplace

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD thematic report draws on the OECD Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) to compare how adults use literacy, numeracy and adaptive problem solving at work across countries. The report describes the survey’s purpose and domains (literacy, numeracy, adaptive problem solving) and uses the resulting cross-country evidence to discuss patterns in skills use and its associations with wages, productivity and well-being. However, the provided text does not specify whether analysts applied PIAAC sampling weights or which weight variable (e.g., student design weights) was used, nor whether replicate weights were used for variance estimation. For policy interpretation, readers should rely on the OECD/PIAAC technical documentation for the recommended complex-survey weighting approach when producing population-representative estimates.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PIAAC thematic report examines how adults use (or do not use) their literacy, numeracy and adaptive problem solving skills in the workplace, and how these patterns relate to wages, productivity and workers’ well-being. It is explicitly framed as a cross-country policy analysis using the latest cycle of the OECD Survey of Adult Skills, highlighting differences in skills use across countries and examining how individual and job characteristics (e.g., gender, educational attainment, occupation) are associated with underutilisation. The excerpt does not provide the statistical model specifications, performance metrics, or any machine-learning pipeline, so no predictive accuracy or effect sizes can be extracted here. Methodologically, the report’s interpretive strength depends on the underlying PIAAC survey design and scaling/estimation procedures, which are not detailed in the provided text. As a result, the excerpt supports qualitative policy conclusions about underutilisation and returns to skills, but it does not allow verification of quantitative estimation choices (e.g., weighting, missing-data treatment, or PV handling).
